David Patient Tribute

By: Kate Barry | Paid

Proposal


Show:

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
We pay tribute to legendary HIV/AIDS survivor, activist and motivational speaker, David Patient

Unique Selling Point:
David Patient conquered his own diagnosis, and brought hope, humor and motivation to thousands of people. As part of the initial AZT trial in the eighties, David proved that an HIV diagnosis wasn't a death sentence.

Summary:
David survived for an astonishing 34 years after his initial diagnosis. In the ned it wasn't the AIDS that killed him. Together with his partner he ran empowerment workshops - teaching people to reach their full potential. He became an inspiration to many, with his uniquely purposeful life.

Further information:
Given up for adoption as a baby, he grew up in a conservative family that struggled to accept his sexuality. Three years ago he reached out to his biological family and met his two sisters who became closely associated with him.

Press Release:


David Patient
South African Aids activist David Patient died last week at the age of 56. Diagnosed as far back
as 1983, Patient was an icon in the age of HIV stigma and an activist for LGBTQI rights. For 34
years he showed that it was possible to live ‘positively’ with HIV. Carte Blanche reflects on his
remarkable will to survive and victory over the idea that his diagnosis was a death sentence.

Script:


DAVID PATIENT TRIBUTE

Text: Well I guess if you are reading this update, I’m history. Yup, I died….finally…shit it took long enough! (if I were you I’d ask for proof!)

V/O On the 23nd of September, with typical irreverence, David Patient announced his own death on Facebook. It was posted by his partner, Neil Orr.

Neil: He wrote a letter. All I had to do was go home, take it off his desktop and put it on. That was him. He was going to manage the whole thing. His life he did his way, his death he did his way too.

V/O: It was 22 years ago when David Patient first sauntered across our screens and into our hearts. A brave, young man fighting impossible odds, challenging a deadly disease that was decimating the population.

David: I have tremendous instincts to survive. I have overcome numerous odds in my life that have put me into a survival frame of mind. And there was no way on hell I was willing to die. Instead of looking at the probability of my dying I started viewing the possibility of my living.

Link: David’s journey goes back to 1983 when he was celebrating his 21st birthday in America. He went to a doctor and got a shattering diagnosis.

V/O: By the time Ruda Landman interviewed him in 1995, he had been living with HIV for 12 years.

Ruda: He was part of the first AZT trials. Every single person who participated in those trials with him died within the next 2 or 3 years.

David: I literally went in and helped people die, sat there with them as they were taking their last breath and stuff. And It wasn’t the big hideous thing that everybody made it out to be. It’s kind alike they invite you in to touch the face of God for a moment, because that’s what it’s about. And there’s nothing like the dying to teach you how to live.

V/O: Ruda and David became lifelong friends

Ruda: He was quite intimidating, because there was that fierce intelligence and a razor-sharp wit, and he didn't just not suffer fools gladly, he did not suffer them. And he would tell you straight to your face that you're taking xyz now.

Link: You can’t really talk about David without including his life partner Neil. Together they made a formidable team with a message of hope they spread far and wide.

V/O: Neil was a psychology student at UCT, researching long-term HIV survivors. They met in 1994.

Neil: I’ve always considered the relationship secondary to what we were doing, and I always kept that in mind. He could do his thing and I could do my thing, but together we could do more.

V/O: Neil was interested in the link between attitude and the immune system. In David he found a living example of how long-term survival depends on a positive outlook.

Neil: And it is still a mystery why, I mean medically it made no sense, and yet there he was. He existed.

David: You’re HIV, I’m David. You’re very powerful and very strong and you can kill me. What I ask you to be Mr HIV is very aware of the fact that I have the same power. I too am strong, I too can take you out, and let’s face it, if I die you die. Now is it realistic or is it unrealistic? I don’t know, but it seems to be working.

V/O: Together they developed a powerful training programme, teaching others what David had learned about living with HIV. One of their trainees was talk show host Criselda Kananda-Dudumashe, who was diagnosed HIV+ while pregnant with her daughter.

Criselda: David instilled a seed of positiveness in me, because at the time I felt so sorry for myself. I wanted the world to acknowledge and understand that I’d been wronged. And he came and asked me a basic question: So what? You’re not unique. Look around, people are going through stuff, it’s called life, it means you’re living. So find ways of dealing with your challenge, and as you connect to your challenge with solutions – not look at me and feel sorry for me.

V/O: They took their training programme Positive Life to Mozambique, one of the poorest nations in the world, with a high prevalence of HIV.

Neil: We were given free rein to create something for the entire country, and we did very quickly. And it was medicine and nutrition and the whole thing, and it still runs to this very day.

Criselda: We’ve been to Namibia together, we’ve been to Swaziland. He taught people how to want food security for themselves, how to plant food gardens. I remember one of his teachings would be many of you have manicured lawns. Are you cows, do you eat grass? It comes out as hilarious, but it’s on point. Many of us don’t have vegetable gardens, what are we being fed? David was not scared of living and he was not scared of dying either. And because of that he embraced his journey with so much humour.

Ruda: He was so funny. I mean one of his last posts from hospital he said "I've just seen a notice above a ward: Stroke Patients. Is that an instruction? Can I be in that Ward? (Laughs)

Link: David was so positive about living for the moment, but never really came to terms with the fact that he was adopted. And in recent years he went on a very different quest: to find his biological family.

V/O: Born in Zambia in 1961, David was given up for adoption when he was just a few weeks old. All attempts to find his birth mother drew a blank. But about 3 years ago he eventually discovered that apart from his adopted sister Debbie, he also had two biological sisters, Tania and Natalie.

Natalie: So, I did not know David existed until three and a half years ago. Well actually I knew David Patient existed but I had no idea that I had a brother called David Patient. My sister actually knew a lot more, because she has worked with Hospice and Lifeline etc. So, she had actually been to one of his talks and she’d gone up and met him afterwards and she had no idea that she was meeting her brother, which was quite an astonishing thing for us when we found out. It was about 5 or 6 years prior to us knowing who he was.

Derek: What first struck you when you met face to face?

Natalie: Actually how much he’s like the family, that was the crazy thing. He did all the right things, he said I’ve got paperwork I can show you who I am. And I just laughed, the first time we met him, he looks so much like my mother.

Derek: And your Mum unfortunately never got to meet him?

Natalie: She passed away 7 years before he found us, so no, that was always a big sadness that he didn’t get to know her. He hoped his mother was desperate and had done it because it was out of her control. Which turned out to be true, it’s not something she wanted to do. She was very, very young and she was forced to do it by her family, she was given no other option.

V/O: Ironically it was not HIV or AIDS that ended David’s life. He developed psoriasis, and the heavy doses of cortisone resulted in hernias, multiple operations and various superbug infections. He died from pneumonia after surgery.

Neil: Part of me is relieved. It was a rough period – two-and-a half years – so I just, I’m actually ok.

David: People often ask me how come you’re in such a good mood all the time? The truth is when I wake up in the morning and I notice that I’m breathing, it’s a fabulous day! No matter what comes to me it’s a great day. And the same thing will happen tomorrow morning, when I wake up and I’m breathing, right on ma, let’s get going, there’s stuff to do.

Text: Don’t squander time… you’re only a breath away from being a corpse yourself. It’s only when time is running out that you really get its value.
